lead: ANOVA tests whether three or more groups have the same mean. Comparing every pair with t-tests would raise the chance of a false alarm. ANOVA splits the total variation of the data into a between-group part and a within-group part, then compares their average sizes with an F ratio. A large F says the group means differ by more than ordinary scatter. One-way ANOVA has one factor; two-way ANOVA has row and column factors. Quality control, agriculture, medicine and any A/B test with several variants use it.
prereq: You need the F ratio from Chapter 6.4, the F distribution from Unit 5, and the null hypothesis idea from Chapter 6.1.

sections.h3: One test instead of many t-tests

blocks.text: A factory checks rod length on k machines. With k=5, pairwise comparison needs 10 t-tests. Each test at α=0.05 has a 5% chance of a false alarm even when all machines are equal. Ten tests make at least one false alarm likely. ANOVA replaces the ten tests with one question: are all k means equal?
The one-way model writes each observation as a sum of three parts.

blocks.where: X<sub>ij</sub> is observation j in group i; μ is the overall mean; τ<sub>i</sub> is the fixed effect of group i, with Στ<sub>i</sub> = 0; ε<sub>ij</sub> is the random error, independent and normal with mean 0 and common variance σ². i = 1, …, k and j = 1, …, n<sub>i</sub>.

blocks.text: The null hypothesis is H0: τ1 = τ2 = … = τk = 0, so all means are equal. The alternative is that at least one τi is not zero. The test uses the F distribution from Chapter 6.4.

sections.h3: Sums of squares, degrees of freedom, F

blocks.text: Let N = n<sub>1</sub> + … + n<sub>k</sub> be the total number of observations. Write X̄<sub>i</sub> for the mean of group i and X̄<sub>··</sub> for the grand mean of all N observations.

blocks.where: SST is the total sum of squares: the squared distance of every observation from the grand mean. It measures all variation in the data.
SSB is the between-group sum of squares. Each group mean is weighted by its sample size n<sub>i</sub>. Some syllabi call it the treatment sum of squares.
SSE is the within-group or error sum of squares: squared distance of each observation from its own group mean.

blocks.text: The three parts obey SST = SSB + SSE. If group means are far apart, SSB is large compared with SSE.

items: State H<sub>0</sub>: all group means equal, and H<sub>1</sub>: at least one differs. Fix α.
Compute the k group means and the grand mean.
Compute SSB and SSE; get SST as their sum or directly.
Degrees of freedom: k − 1 for between, N − k for within, N − 1 for total.
Mean squares: MSB = SSB/(k − 1) and MSE = SSE/(N − k).
F = MSB/MSE. Compare with the critical value F<sub>α</sub>(k − 1, N − k). Reject H<sub>0</sub> if F is larger.
Errors are normal with mean 0 and the same variance σ² in every group.
Group effects add; there is no interaction in one-way ANOVA.
The F test is fairly robust to mild non-normality when group sizes are equal.

blocks.text: Two-way ANOVA studies two factors at once. A row factor has r levels and a column factor has c levels. One observation is taken in each row-column cell, so there are rc observations. Example: r machines and c operators, one rod from each machine-operator pair.

blocks.where: X<sub>ij</sub> is the observation in row i and column j; μ is the overall mean; α<sub>i</sub> is the row effect; β<sub>j</sub> is the column effect; ε<sub>ij</sub> is the error, independent normal with mean 0 and variance σ².

blocks.text: The model has no interaction term. It assumes the row effect is the same at every column and the column effect is the same at every row. Without repeated observations in each cell, interaction cannot be separated from error.
SS<sub>row</sub> = c Σ<sub>i</sub> (X̄<sub>i·</sub> − X̄<sub>··</sub>)², SS<sub>col</sub> = r Σ<sub>j</sub> (X̄<sub>·j</sub> − X̄<sub>··</sub>)²
blocks.where: SS<sub>row</sub> measures row-mean differences; SS<sub>col</sub> measures column-mean differences; X̄<sub>i·</sub> is row i mean, X̄<sub>·j</sub> is column j mean. SSE = SST − SS<sub>row</sub> − SS<sub>col</sub>.

items: Degrees of freedom: r − 1 for rows, c − 1 for columns, (r − 1)(c − 1) for error, rc − 1 for total.
Mean squares: MS<sub>row</sub> = SS<sub>row</sub>/(r − 1), MS<sub>col</sub> = SS<sub>col</sub>/(c − 1), MSE = SSE/[(r − 1)(c − 1)].
Test rows with F = MS<sub>row</sub>/MSE and columns with F = MS<sub>col</sub>/MSE.
Compare each F with its critical value using the error degrees of freedom.

blocks.text: Interaction needs replication in each cell and is covered only by a few universities. Post-hoc comparisons after a significant F are also beyond this chapter.

examples.question: Three machines make rods. Four rod lengths (mm) per machine are M1: 9, 10, 11, 10; M2: 11, 12, 13, 12; M3: 13, 14, 15, 14. Test at α = 0.05 whether the mean rod lengths are equal. Use one-way ANOVA.
steps: H<sub>0</sub>: μ<sub>1</sub> = μ<sub>2</sub> = μ<sub>3</sub>; H<sub>1</sub>: at least one mean differs. α = 0.05.
Group means: M1 mean = 40/4 = 10 mm; M2 mean = 48/4 = 12 mm; M3 mean = 56/4 = 14 mm. Grand mean = 144/12 = 12 mm.
SSE: M1 deviations −1, 0, 1, 0 give squares 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2; M2 gives 2; M3 gives 2. SSE = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 mm². SST = SSB + SSE = 38 mm².
df between = k − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2. df within = N − k = 12 − 3 = 9. df total = 11.
The critical value F(0.05, 2, 9) = 4.26. Since 24 > 4.26, reject H<sub>0</sub>.
examples.answer: Reject equality of means; the three machines do not have the same mean rod length at the 5% level.
examples.check:
data = [[9,10,11,10],[11,12,13,12],[13,14,15,14]]
k = len(data)
N = sum(len(g) for g in data)
grand = sum(sum(g) for g in data) / N
means = [sum(g)/len(g) for g in data]
ssb = sum(len(g)*(m-grand)**2 for g, m in zip(data, means))
sse = sum((x-m)**2 for g, m in zip(data, means) for x in g)
sst = ssb + sse
dfb = k - 1
dfe = N - k
msb = ssb / dfb
mse = sse / dfe
F = msb / mse
print(ssb)
print(sse)
print(sst)
print(dfb)
print(dfe)
print(msb)
print(mse)
print(F)
print(4.26)

traps: Use k − 1 and N − k. Swapping them gives the wrong F and the wrong table look-up.
Do not run repeated t-tests for three or more means; the chance of at least one type I error grows with the number of tests.
SSB and SSE are sums of squares (mm²); MSB and MSE are mean squares (mm²); F is a ratio with no units.
In two-way ANOVA without replication, an apparent interaction cannot be tested; it is mixed into the error.
A large F rejects equality of means but does not say which mean differs. That needs a post-hoc test.

quiz.q: In one-way ANOVA with k groups and N observations, what are the degrees of freedom for SSB, SSE and SST?
quiz.a: k − 1 for SSB, N − k for SSE, and N − 1 for SST.

quiz.q: Why is one ANOVA F test preferred to all pairwise t-tests for five group means?
quiz.a: Ten t-tests at 5% each make at least one false rejection likely; one F test controls α at 5% for the single question of equal means.

quiz.q: Four groups, six observations each, SSB = 60 and SSE = 100. Compute MSB, MSE and F.
In a two-way classification r = 3, c = 4, no replication, SST = 200, SS_row = 60, SS_col = 80. Find SSE, error df, MSE, and F_row.
A one-way ANOVA gives F = 1.2 with df (2, 15); the 5% critical value is 3.68. What is the decision? What does it mean?
quiz.a: Fail to reject H0. There is no significant evidence that the group means differ; it does not prove they are equal.

quiz.q: An ANOVA table shows a large F for rows and a small F for columns. Write the conclusion in plain words.
quiz.a: The row factor is associated with a significant difference in means; the column factor is not. The two conclusions are separate.

quiz.q: Write the one-way ANOVA model and define its three terms.
quiz.a: X_ij = μ + τ_i + ε_ij; μ is the overall mean, τ_i is the group effect, and ε_ij is a normal error with mean 0 and variance σ².

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, ANOVA is the backbone of design of experiments and Six Sigma. A/B tests with several variants use one-way ANOVA or its regression form. Clinical trials use two-way and repeated-measures ANOVA to remove patient and period effects. Newer courses add random effects, mixed models and Tukey HSD for post-hoc comparisons. Search for 'Tukey HSD', 'two-way ANOVA with interaction' and 'design of experiments'.
